title: Replication and partitioning
description: Learn about data replication and partitioning strategies for scaling databases and distributed systems.

data.text: Replication and partitioning are fundamental techniques for scaling data storage. Replication copies data across multiple nodes for availability and performance, while partitioning splits data across nodes to distribute load.
Replication maintains multiple copies of the same data on different machines. This improves read performance, provides fault tolerance, and enables geographic distribution.

items: Master-slave (leader-follower)—writes go to primary, reads from replicas
Multi-master—writes allowed on any node, requires conflict resolution
Chain replication—reduces leader load, longer latency for consistency
Quorum-based—majority agreement for writes and reads

items.title: Synchronous Replication
items.description: Strong consistency but slower writes. Leader waits for replicas to acknowledge before confirming writes. Higher latency, better data safety.

items.title: Asynchronous Replication
items.description: Fast writes but eventual consistency. Leader confirms writes immediately, replicas catch up later. Lower latency, risk of data loss on failure.

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: Use synchronous replication for critical data and asynchronous for non-critical data. Many systems use a hybrid approach with configurable consistency levels.
Partitioning splits a large dataset into smaller chunks distributed across multiple nodes. Each node holds a subset of the data, distributing both storage and computational load.

items: Horizontal partitioning (sharding)—rows distributed by key
Vertical partitioning—columns split across nodes (different tables)
Range-based—data ranges assigned to shards (e.g., A-M, N-Z)
Hash-based—consistent hash of key determines shard
Directory-based—lookup service maps keys to shards
Rebalancing—moving data when adding/removing shards
Hotspots—uneven distribution causing overloaded shards
Cross-shard queries—expensive joins across partitions
Skewed workloads—some shards get more traffic than others
Operational complexity—managing many database instances

data.text: These techniques often work together rather than in isolation.

items: Start with replication for read scaling and availability
Add partitioning when a single node can't hold all data
Use replication within each partition for fault tolerance
Consider geographic replication for global applications
Combine both: partition data, then replicate each partition

data.title: Caution
data.text: Don't partition too early. Replication solves many problems and is simpler. Only partition when you've outgrown a single node's capacity.

items: Choosing the wrong partitioning key leading to hotspots
Not planning for rebalancing when data grows
Ignoring cross-partition query performance
Underestimating operational overhead of many partitions
Failing to handle partition failures gracefully
